newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea wage hike may lead to job cuts - employers.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea wage hike may lead to job cuts - employers.

text.p: South Korea's main employer group said on Wednesday that workers would have to sacrifice large wage increases this year in order to maintain job stability.

The Korea Employers Federation (KEF), which represents large conglomerates, said in a statement that its position on this year's wage negotiations takes into account the more than $3 billion in production losses from recent strikes.
"If wage increases are too big, companies will be forced to lay off workers," said KFE spokesman Choi Jae-hwang. "For job stability, we hope workers won't demand high increases."
South Korea was wracked by work stoppages for almost four weeks until January 20 over a labour law rammed through parliament in December in the absence of opposition politicians.

The law would let employers lay off workers, hire part-time staff and introduce flexible working hours. President Kim Young-sam sent the legislation back to parliament to be revised after the strikes hurt South Korea's already frail economy.
The KFE statement said that "wage negotiations will be based on job stability, and no bonus increase or additional welfare benifits will be added".
It also suggested that salaries be based on ability rather than on length of employment, a foreign concept to most Korean workers.
"Korea's economy is going through difficult times. We have taken this into consideration and hope workers will do the same," said Choi.
The group's wage stance signaled new feuding between management and unions.
The Federation of Korean Trade Unions said on Friday it would seek an average 11.2 percent wage increase taking into account the rise in the cost of living, estimated at 4.5 percent in 1996.

The federation, a government-sanctioned union with 1.2 million members that largely avoided the recent strikes, said it would seek an additional 7.2 percent wage increase unless the labour law revisions conformed with international standards.
The KFE plans to announce a specific wage increase offer on February 25. Negotiations with workers usually begin at the end of February, although no specific date has yet been set.
Over the past decade, wages in South Korea have increased by an average of 15 percent annually.
